definition: A group of networked computers (nodes) that work together as one system, such as the 3 or 5 machines that make up an etcd or Cassandra deployment.
example: A five-node Raft cluster keeps working as long as three of its machines can talk to each other.

definition: A failure where some parts of a distributed system stop working while others carry on, and some are in an unknown state. Unlike a single machine, which usually fails completely, a distributed system must keep running and reasoning while parts of it are broken.
example: One of three database replicas loses power while the other two keep serving requests.

definition: An algorithm or command that always produces the same output and state changes from the same input and starting state, with no randomness. State machine replication relies on commands being deterministic so every replica ends in the same state.
example: "Set x to 5" is deterministic; "set x to a random number" is not, so replicas applying it would diverge.

definition: A change an operation makes to the outside world beyond returning a result, such as charging a card, sending an email or writing to a database. Side effects are why a duplicated retry can be harmful.
example: Charging a card twice because a retry was processed twice is a duplicated side effect.

definition: A unique identifier a client sends with a request so the server can recognise a retry of the same operation and return the original result instead of doing the work again. The key must identify the operation (for example the order), not the attempt.
example: Sending key "order-77:charge" with every retry of a payment means the card is charged at most once.

definition: The part of a distributed system that decides whether another node is alive, usually by watching for heartbeats or replies within a timeout. Because a slow node and a dead node look the same, every failure detector is a guess that can be wrong.
example: A detector that marks a node dead after 1 second of silence will wrongly accuse nodes that have 2-second pauses.

definition: A failure detector (Hayashibara et al., 2004) that outputs a continuous suspicion level, phi (φ), instead of a yes/no verdict. Phi grows the longer a node stays silent compared with its usual heartbeat pattern, and the application chooses the threshold at which to act. Cassandra and Akka use it.
example: Cassandra declares a node down when its phi passes phi_convict_threshold, 8 by default.

definition: Randomness added to retry wait times so that many clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same moment. Without it, retries arrive in synchronised waves that can knock a recovering server over again.
example: Instead of every client waiting exactly 400 ms, each waits a random time between 0 and 400 ms.

definition: The multiplication of load when several layers of a system each retry failed calls independently. With L layers each making a attempts, one user request can turn into a to the power L calls at the bottom.
example: Three layers that each try 3 times can send 27 calls to a database that is already failing.

definition: A network, such as Ethernet, IP or the internet, that splits data into packets and promises nothing about when (or whether) each one arrives. Packets can be dropped, delayed, duplicated or reordered.

A device that connects machines on a local network and forwards packets between them. When packets arrive faster than it can forward them, they wait in its buffer, and when the buffer is full, they are dropped.
The standard family of technologies for wired local area networks, used to connect servers in almost every data centre. It delivers frames on a best-effort basis with no guaranteed delivery time.
The TCP flag a side sends to say it has finished sending and wants to close the connection. Each side sends a FIN and acknowledges the other’s.

The TCP state that the side which closes a connection first stays in for a while, so it can re-send the final ACK if the peer's FIN is retransmitted and so stray old packets die out. The original TCP specification sets it to twice the maximum segment lifetime (2 × 2 minutes = 4 minutes); Linux uses a fixed 60 seconds.
A theoretical timing model that assumes known upper bounds on message delay, processing time and clock drift. Algorithms are easy to design in it, but real networks don’t guarantee those bounds.

A timing model in which the network and processes usually behave within bounds, but the bounds can be broken for a while. Practical consensus algorithms such as Raft and Paxos assume it: they stay safe always and make progress once timing behaves.

A timing model with no bounds at all on message delay or processing speed: a message is eventually delivered, but could take any amount of time. The FLP result shows deterministic consensus cannot guarantee termination in it.

How fast a clock runs fast or slow compared with true time, usually measured in parts per million (ppm). Quartz clocks in servers typically drift by tens of ppm, and the rate changes with temperature. Skew is the gap this builds up between two clocks.
example: 200 ppm of drift adds up to about 17 seconds a day.

definition: A guarantee that something bad never happens, such as "two nodes never decide different values" or "there are never two leaders in one term". A safety violation is a single bad event you could point to.

A guarantee that something good eventually happens, such as "a leader is eventually elected" or "every request eventually gets an answer". Practical algorithms usually guarantee safety always and liveness only when the network behaves.

A partition where messages get through in one direction but not the other, for example a network card that drops only inbound packets. The two sides then reach contradictory conclusions about who is alive.
A clock that counts the vibrations of a small quartz crystal. Every server has one; it is cheap and fairly stable but runs slightly fast or slow, and its rate changes with temperature.
A way of writing very small fractions: 1 ppm is one millionth (0.000001). For clocks it measures drift: 1 ppm means gaining or losing 1 microsecond every second.
example: 200 ppm × 86,400 seconds in a day ≈ 17 seconds of drift per day.

definition: The standard internet protocol for synchronising computer clocks with time servers. It estimates the offset from a round trip of four timestamps and typically keeps clocks within about a millisecond on a good LAN and tens of milliseconds over the internet.
A network covering a small area such as one building or data centre, with low delay (often well under a millisecond between machines).
A network spanning large distances, such as between cities or regions. Round trips take tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so chatty protocols become slow over a WAN.
example: London to Virginia is roughly 75 ms round trip.

definition: A period in which a running program stops executing without realising it, caused by garbage collection, a virtual machine being suspended or migrated, memory swapping or a laptop going to sleep. When it resumes, its idea of the time and of what it holds may be out of date.
Moving a running virtual machine from one physical host to another. The guest is briefly frozen, which looks to other nodes like a pause.

When the operating system runs short of RAM and moves some of a process’s memory out to disk, then back when it is needed. Accessing swapped-out memory is thousands of times slower, so a process can stall.

A lock or role that is granted for a limited time and must be renewed to be kept. If the holder crashes, renewals stop and the lease expires, letting someone else take over. Every practical distributed lock is really a lease.
example: A leader holds a 10-second lease and renews it every 3 seconds.

definition: The node that coordinates writes for a group of replicas: clients send writes to it, it decides their order and sends them to the followers. Raft, Kafka and most databases elect one leader at a time.

The process by which a group of nodes chooses exactly one of them to act as leader, and chooses a new one when the leader fails. It is a lock on the role "leader", so it needs consensus or a consensus-backed lock service.

Eight false assumptions newcomers make about networks, listed by Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn’t change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous.
A US computer company (1982–2010, then acquired by Oracle) that made servers and workstations and created Java. Its engineers compiled the fallacies of distributed computing.
An interface that needs many small back-and-forth requests to get one job done. Each request pays a network round trip, so chatty APIs are fine inside a data centre and slow across a WAN.
The actual data carried in a message or request, as opposed to the headers and metadata around it.
The layout of a network: which machines and links connect to which. It changes when servers fail over, move or scale, which breaks hard-coded addresses.

A thought experiment showing that two parties communicating over a channel that can lose messages can never be certain they agree. Whatever message is sent last might be lost, so its sender can’t rely on it.

A problem posed by Lamport, Shostak and Pease (1982): reaching agreement when some participants may lie or behave arbitrarily. With ordinary (unsigned) messages it needs at least 3f + 1 participants to tolerate f traitors.

A fault where a node behaves arbitrarily: it may lie, send different answers to different nodes or corrupt data, not just stop. Tolerating Byzantine faults is expensive, so most systems inside one company assume nodes only crash.
A consensus algorithm (Castro and Liskov, 1999) that tolerates f Byzantine nodes out of 3f + 1. It and its descendants are used in some blockchains and high-assurance systems.

Describes a system that keeps working correctly even when some nodes behave arbitrarily or maliciously. Practical BFT consensus protocols such as PBFT need 3f + 1 nodes to tolerate f faulty ones, so they come in sizes such as 4, 7 and 10.
A fault model in which a node fails by halting and never comes back. It is the simplest model to reason about.
A fault model in which a node may halt and later restart, keeping whatever it had saved to durable storage. Raft and Paxos assume this model.
A fault model in which a node keeps running but fails to send or receive some messages.

The assumptions an algorithm makes about how components can fail: for example only by stopping (crash), by stopping and restarting (crash-recovery), or arbitrarily (Byzantine). An algorithm’s guarantees hold only for failures inside its model.
Storage whose contents survive a crash or power cut, such as a disk after an fsync. Consensus algorithms must write votes and log entries durably before acting on them.

When a node restarts having lost state it promised was durable, for example with an empty or rolled-back disk. It falls outside the crash-recovery model: the node may vote twice or forget committed data, breaking safety.
A small value computed from a block of data and stored with it. Recomputing and comparing it later detects corruption.
Data that changes on disk or in memory without any error being reported, for example a flipped bit. A node serving corrupted data behaves more like a Byzantine node than a crashed one.
A partial or subtle failure in which a component looks healthy to some observers or checks but is not doing its job, such as a node that sends heartbeats but can’t receive requests.
A small message a node sends regularly to say "I’m alive". Other nodes treat a long gap in heartbeats as a sign of failure.
example: By default an etcd leader sends a heartbeat every 100 ms, and a follower starts an election after 1,000 ms without one.

definition: Asking other nodes to contact a suspect node on your behalf. If they can reach it, the problem was your own network path, not the suspect.

Adding nodes to, or removing them from, a replicated group. In consensus systems it must be done carefully, one node at a time or with joint consensus, so that old and new majorities can’t decide different things.
A way of proving something impossible: assume it is possible, follow the logic, and reach a result that can’t be true. The assumption must therefore be false.
A company or service that carries out card payments for merchants, such as Stripe or Adyen. Its API is an external resource that won’t check your fencing tokens, so it needs idempotency keys.
Memory in the operating system that holds data waiting to be sent or read on a network connection. A write can sit there and arrive at the far end well after the program thinks it sent it.
A replicated, append-only ledger kept by many mutually untrusting parties, who agree on new blocks using a Byzantine-fault-tolerant protocol.
The list of which nodes currently belong to a cluster and which are alive. Gossip protocols such as SWIM spread membership changes; ZooKeeper offers it as a recipe.
Declaring a healthy node dead. Short timeouts produce more false positives; each one can trigger needless failovers and rebalancing.
The record of every operation clients performed on a system, with when each started and finished and what it returned. A consistency model is defined by which histories it allows.
The promise that once a write has completed, every later read sees it or something newer. It is the key practical consequence of linearizability.
The single instant, somewhere between an operation’s start and end, at which a linearizable system behaves as if the operation took effect.

The property that if each object on its own satisfies a consistency model, the whole system of objects does too. Linearizability composes, so keys can be sharded across independent groups; sequential consistency does not.
A consistency model (Lamport, 1979) in which all operations appear in one single order that every client agrees on and that respects each client’s own program order, but not necessarily real time.
The order in which one client (or thread) issued its own operations. Sequential consistency must respect it; different clients’ operations may be interleaved in any order.
An ordering in which every pair of items is ranked one before the other, so everything lines up in one sequence. Logs and consensus produce a total order of operations.
The relation between two events when one could have influenced the other, for example because a client read A’s result before doing B. Causal order is the order such dependencies impose.

Events or writes where neither could have influenced the other: neither happened before the other. They need not happen at the same moment; they just have no causal link. Concurrent writes to the same data are what conflict resolution has to merge.
example: Two users who edit the same cart without seeing each other’s change make concurrent writes, even if the edits are seconds apart.

definition: Microsoft’s globally distributed database service, which offers five named consistency levels from strong to eventual, including bounded staleness and session consistency.

Four cheap guarantees, defined by Terry et al. for the Bayou system in 1994, that make an eventually consistent store behave sensibly for each client session: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads.
A session guarantee that once a client has seen a value, later reads never return an older one: time never appears to go backwards for that client.
example: A comment thread never shows 12 comments, then 9, then 12 again.

definition: A session guarantee that a client’s writes are applied everywhere in the order the client made them.
A session guarantee that a write a client makes after reading a value is ordered after the write that produced that value.
A research replicated storage system from Xerox PARC in the 1990s, designed for mobile devices that are often disconnected. Its papers introduced the session guarantees.
A number identifying a position in a database’s write-ahead log. Comparing LSNs tells you whether a replica has caught up to a given write.
example: A client that wrote at LSN 5,000 only reads from replicas at LSN 5,000 or beyond.

definition: A guarantee for transactions: the outcome is the same as if they had run one at a time in some order. That order need not match real time.
Serializability plus real-time order: if one transaction finishes before another starts, it must come first in the serial order. It is the transactional version of linearizability.
Google’s globally distributed SQL database. It replicates data with Paxos, runs two-phase commit across shards, and uses TrueTime to give strictly serializable transactions.
An open-source distributed key-value database, now maintained by Apple, that provides strictly serializable transactions.
A project by Kyle Kingsbury that tests real databases under network partitions and clock faults and publishes analyses. It has repeatedly found systems that violate the consistency they advertise.
A rule that no two records may have the same value in some field, such as a username. Enforcing it across replicas needs every replica to agree on the latest state, so it needs linearizability.
An atomic operation that changes a value only if it still equals an expected value, and reports whether it did. It lets two clients race safely: only one of them wins.
example: Set username "alice" only if it is currently unclaimed; the second registration fails.

definition: Availability that holds only as long as each client keeps talking to the same replica. Causal consistency can stay available during partitions under this assumption.

An anomaly in which a transaction sees the effect of a later transaction but not of an earlier one that finished before it began. Serializable systems without real-time ordering can allow it; strict serializability forbids it.
A read that returns data as of a particular point in time, ignoring later changes. Served from a lagging replica, it can return stale data.
An order in which transactions run strictly one after another with no overlap. A serializable system’s results must match some serial order.
A transaction that only reads data and writes nothing, such as a report or an audit query.
One client’s sequence of interactions with a system, often identified by a token or connection. Session guarantees hold within a session, not across clients.
The clock that reports the calendar date and time (on Linux, CLOCK_REALTIME). NTP can step it forwards or backwards, so it must not be used to measure durations.

A clock that only ever moves forward, counting from an arbitrary starting point such as boot. It is the right clock for measuring durations and timeouts on one machine, but its values mean nothing on another machine.
example: Python’s time.monotonic() and Java’s System.nanoTime() read a monotonic clock.

definition: A level in NTP’s hierarchy of time sources. Stratum 0 is a reference clock such as an atomic clock or GPS receiver; stratum 1 servers attach directly to one; each further level syncs from the level above.
A highly accurate clock that keeps time using the vibrations of atoms, typically caesium or rubidium. Google’s time masters use them alongside GPS.
The US satellite navigation system. Its satellites carry atomic clocks, so a GPS receiver is also an accurate time source for data centres.
How far one clock is ahead of or behind another (or true time). NTP estimates it; CockroachDB sets a maximum allowed offset (500 ms by default) between any two nodes.
Correcting a clock gradually by running it slightly fast or slow until it matches, so it never jumps. NTP slews small offsets.
Correcting a clock by jumping it straight to the right time. NTP steps large offsets; a backward step is how a time-of-day clock goes backwards.
Spreading a leap second over many hours by running clocks very slightly slow or fast, instead of inserting an extra second at once. Google and AWS time services do this.

A conflict-resolution rule that keeps the write with the highest timestamp and silently discards the others. Simple and convergent, but it loses concurrent writes, and clock skew can make it discard the genuinely later one.

Lamport’s ordering of events without clocks: a happens before b (written a → b) if they are on the same process in that order, if a sends a message that b receives, or through a chain of such steps. If neither happens before the other, they are concurrent.
The property that if a relates to b and b relates to c, then a relates to c. Happens-before is transitive: a → b and b → c give a → c.

A logical clock (Lamport, 1978): each process keeps a counter, adds one for each event, and on receiving a message jumps past the message’s counter. If a happened before b, a’s timestamp is smaller, but a smaller timestamp doesn’t prove a happened first.
example: P1 at 7 sends a message stamped 8; P2 at 3 receives it and moves to 9.

definition: A counter used to order events by cause and effect rather than by physical time. Lamport clocks, vector clocks, Raft terms and Paxos ballot numbers are all logical clocks.

A numbered period of time in Raft, starting with an election. Each term has at most one leader, every message carries the sender’s term, and a node that sees a higher term steps down to follower. It acts as a logical clock and a fencing token.
The unique, increasing number a Paxos proposer attaches to each attempt to get a value chosen. Acceptors promise to ignore lower numbers, which makes it act like a logical clock.
A number Kafka increases each time a partition gets a new leader. Replicas use it to detect and discard data from an old leader.
The 64-bit id ZooKeeper gives every change. Its high 32 bits are the leader’s epoch and its low 32 bits a counter, so it only ever increases and can be used as a fencing token.
Two or more concurrent versions of the same key that a store such as Riak keeps side by side instead of picking one. The next reader receives them all and must merge them.
An open-source, Dynamo-style distributed key-value store. It uses sloppy quorums by default, keeps concurrent versions as siblings, and offers CRDT data types.

A clock (Kulkarni et al., 2014) whose timestamps pair the largest physical time seen with a small counter. It respects happens-before like a Lamport clock while staying close to real time. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use it.
An open-source distributed SQL database that replicates data with Raft and uses hybrid logical clocks for transaction timestamps.

In CockroachDB, the window just above a read’s timestamp, as wide as the maximum clock offset, in which a value might have been written before the read in real time. A read that meets such a value restarts at a higher timestamp.
example: With a 500 ms maximum offset, a read at 10.000 s that finds a value at 10.200 s restarts.

definition: In Spanner, a server in each data centre with a GPS receiver or atomic clock that other machines poll to keep their TrueTime uncertainty small.

Spanner’s rule of waiting, after choosing a commit timestamp, until TrueTime guarantees that timestamp is in the past everywhere. It takes about twice TrueTime’s error bound and gives external consistency.
example: With an error bound of 4 ms, commit wait is about 8 ms.

definition: TrueTime’s epsilon (ε): how far the local clock might be from true time in either direction. In the 2012 Spanner paper it varied between about 1 and 7 ms, growing between synchronisations with the time masters.
When a calculation produces a number too large for the space reserved for it, so it wraps around to a very small or negative value.
example: A signed 64-bit count of nanoseconds overflows after about 292 years.

definition: A CPU technique of running instructions in a different order from the program when that is faster, while making the results look as if they ran in order. It is invisible to a program reading a clock.
A permanent record of who did what and when, kept for security or compliance. Its timestamps must be calendar times that people can read.
The guarantee that at most one process at a time is inside a critical section or holds a lock.

Replication with no single leader: a client (or a coordinator acting for it) sends each write to several replicas in parallel and counts it done once enough acknowledge. Popularised by Amazon’s Dynamo; used by Cassandra and Riak.
Replication in which every write goes through one leader, which orders writes and forwards them to followers.
An open-source database compatible with Cassandra, rewritten in C++ for higher performance.
An open-source Dynamo-style key-value store originally built at LinkedIn.

The node that drives one operation on behalf of a client: in a Dynamo-style store it forwards a read or write to the replicas and gathers their answers; in two-phase commit it collects votes and decides commit or abort.
In a Dynamo-style store, the ordered list of nodes responsible for a key: the next N distinct nodes clockwise from the key’s position on the hash ring.
The sets of replicas that must respond for a write (W of them) or a read (R of them) to count as successful. Their sizes decide whether reads are guaranteed to meet the latest write.
The condition R + W > N: when the replicas a read hears from plus the replicas a write reached add up to more than the total, every read set shares at least one replica with every write set.
example: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2: 2 + 2 = 4, which is more than 3, so reads always meet the latest write.

definition: Cassandra consistency levels for clusters that span several data centres. LOCAL_QUORUM needs a majority of the replicas in the coordinator's own data centre, avoiding cross-region round trips; EACH_QUORUM needs a majority in every data centre.
example: With 3 replicas in each of two data centres, LOCAL_QUORUM waits for 2 local replicas; EACH_QUORUM waits for 2 in each.

definition: A quorum algorithm (Attiya, Bar-Noy and Dolev, 1995) that makes a replicated read/write register linearizable without a leader: writers first read the highest version from a quorum, and readers write back what they read before returning.
The simplest replicated object: a single value that supports read and write (overwrite), with no compare-and-set. Quorum algorithms like ABD can make a register linearizable without consensus.

An operation that reads a value, computes a new one from it and writes it back, such as incrementing a counter. Doing it safely under concurrency needs an atomic operation such as compare-and-set, or consensus in a distributed system.
Cassandra’s conditional writes (for example INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS), implemented with a Paxos round so that compare-and-set is linearizable.
A form of read repair in which the coordinator waits for stale replicas to be updated before returning the result, so a later read cannot see an older value (monotonic quorum reads).

A model by Peter Bailis and colleagues (VLDB 2012) that predicts how likely an eventually consistent quorum read is to return the latest value, given measured latencies. It showed partial quorums are usually fresh within milliseconds.
A quorum that accepts writes on healthy nodes outside a key’s preference list when the proper replicas are unreachable. It keeps writes available but breaks the guarantee that reads overlap writes.
A quorum counted only from the replicas that actually own the key, with no stand-in nodes, so R + W > N really does guarantee overlap.
When a stand-in node accepts a write meant for an unreachable replica, it stores it with a "hint" naming the owner and hands it over when the owner comes back.
In Cassandra, how long coordinators keep storing hints for a down replica: 3 hours by default. Writes after that are not hinted, so a replica down for longer needs repair.
Fixing stale replicas during a read: when the replicas asked return different versions, the coordinator sends the newest version to the stale ones. It only fixes keys that are read.
example: A read gets v7, v7 and v5; it returns v7 and writes v7 to the replica that had v5.

definition: A background process that compares replicas and copies over any missing or newer data, so even keys that are never read converge. Dynamo-style stores use Merkle trees to make the comparison cheap.

A tree in which each leaf holds the hash of a block of data and each parent holds the hash of its children. Two replicas compare root hashes and descend only into subtrees that differ, finding differences with few comparisons.
example: With about a million leaves, finding one differing leaf takes about 20 levels of comparisons.

definition: The Cassandra command that runs anti-entropy repair: replicas build Merkle trees per token range, compare them and stream differences.
A contiguous slice of the hash ring (in Cassandra, of token values) owned by a set of replicas. Repair and data movement work range by range.
The Cassandra table setting for how long tombstones are kept before compaction may purge them: 864,000 seconds (10 days) by default. Repair must run within this window or deleted data can come back.
When deleted data reappears because a replica that missed the delete still has the old value after the tombstone has been purged elsewhere. Read repair or anti-entropy then copies the old value back.
Background work that rewrites stored data to drop overwritten values and expired tombstones and reclaim space. In Raft, log compaction replaces the start of the log with a snapshot.
A tree in which each node has at most two children. Halving at each level means a tree over n leaves is about log₂(n) levels deep.

Keeping replicas identical by having each start in the same state and apply the same deterministic commands in the same order. Consensus decides the order; etcd, ZooKeeper and CockroachDB work this way.
An ordered list of commands copied to every replica, agreed entry by entry with consensus. Applying it in order gives state machine replication.

The liveness property of consensus: every node that doesn’t fail eventually decides a value. Agreement (no two nodes decide differently), validity (the value was proposed) and integrity (each node decides once) are the safety properties.
HashiCorp’s service-discovery and configuration tool. Its servers agree on data with Raft, and its agents track membership with SWIM-style gossip.
Kafka’s built-in Raft-based metadata system, which replaced ZooKeeper. Kafka 4.0 (2025) runs only in KRaft mode.
An open-source distributed transactional key-value store that splits data into regions, each replicated with Raft.

A 1985 result by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson: in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic algorithm can guarantee to reach consensus if even one process may crash. Practical algorithms escape it with timeouts (partial synchrony) or randomness.
In the FLP proof, a state of the system from which either decision is still possible. The proof shows an algorithm can be kept in such states forever.
In impossibility proofs, an imagined opponent that chooses the worst possible order and timing of message deliveries, within the model’s rules.
Consensus algorithms that use random choices to escape FLP: they never violate safety and terminate with probability 1. Ben-Or’s 1983 protocol was the first.
A Raft node that has stopped hearing from a leader, increased its term, voted for itself and asked the others for votes. It becomes leader with votes from a majority.
The Raft message a leader sends to copy log entries to followers. It includes the index and term of the preceding entry for the consistency check, and the empty version serves as a heartbeat.
The Raft message a candidate sends to ask for votes, carrying its term and the index and term of its last log entry.
The Raft message a leader sends to a follower so far behind that the entries it needs have been compacted away; the follower loads the snapshot instead.
How long a Raft follower waits without hearing from a leader before starting an election. It is randomised (the Raft paper suggests 150–300 ms) so nodes rarely start at once.
A Raft election in which no candidate gets a majority, usually because several started at once. Candidates time out and try again in a new term.

Raft’s rule that a node votes only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own: the last entry’s term is higher, or equal with a log at least as long. It guarantees a new leader has every committed entry.
One record in a replicated log. In Raft each entry has an index (its position), a term (when it was created) and a command.
The position of an entry in a replicated log, counting from 1.
The highest log index a Raft node knows to be committed. Followers learn it from the leader and apply entries up to it.

When a follower receives AppendEntries, it accepts only if its log has an entry at the preceding index with the same term. On failure the leader retries further back until they match, then overwrites the follower’s conflicting entries.
A log entry that is stored on a majority and is guaranteed never to be lost or changed, so it is safe to apply. Raft commits only entries from the leader’s current term by counting replicas.
Raft’s guarantee that if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up to that index.
Raft’s guarantee that a committed entry will be in the log of every future leader, because any winning majority overlaps the majority that stored it.
An entry that does nothing when applied. A new Raft leader appends one at the start of its term so that committing it also commits every earlier entry.

The diagram in the Raft paper showing that an entry from an older term can be on a majority and still be overwritten, which is why leaders only commit entries from their own term by counting replicas.

A way for a Raft leader to serve a linearizable read without writing to the log: record the commit index, confirm it is still leader with a round of heartbeats to a majority, wait until it has applied up to that index, then read. etcd uses it.
A period during which a leader assumes no other leader can exist, letting it serve reads locally with no round trip. It is safe only if clocks run at nearly the same rate.

A Raft extension in which a node asks whether it could win before increasing its term. An isolated node never gets a majority of pre-votes, so it can’t inflate its term and disrupt the cluster when it reconnects.
A Raft extension in which a leader steps down if it hasn’t heard from a majority within an election timeout, so a leader cut off in a minority stops accepting writes.
Raft’s method for changing many members at once: for a transition period decisions need majorities of both the old and the new configuration, so the two can’t decide independently.
A saved copy of a state machine’s state at some log index, which lets everything before that index be deleted from the log.
The basic Paxos protocol, which agrees on one value in two phases: prepare/promise, then accept/accepted.
The Paxos role that tries to get a value chosen by sending Prepare and Accept messages with a proposal number.
The Paxos role that votes: it promises to ignore lower-numbered proposals and accepts values. A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors accept it.
Paxos run for a sequence of log slots with a stable leader that skips the prepare phase for later slots, making it similar to Raft.
Google’s Paxos-based lock service (Burrows, 2006). Its paper introduced the sequencer, the idea behind fencing tokens.
A cluster-wide counter etcd increases on every change. Each key records the revision when it was created (create_revision) and last modified (mod_revision), which makes them natural fencing tokens.
Delivering messages to all nodes reliably and in the same order. It is equivalent to consensus.

A node in ZooKeeper’s tree of data. Ephemeral znodes are deleted when the session that created them ends; sequential znodes get an increasing number appended to their name. Together they give leader election and lock recipes.
example: /election/n_0000000042 is an ephemeral sequential znode.

definition: The connection state between a ZooKeeper client and the ensemble, kept alive by heartbeats. If it expires, the client’s ephemeral znodes are deleted, releasing any leadership or lock they represented.
When many waiting clients are all woken by one event and rush to act at once, though only one can succeed. ZooKeeper recipes avoid it by having each client watch only its predecessor.

A service that hands out distributed locks, which processes on different machines use so that only one of them acts at a time. ZooKeeper, etcd and Google's Chubby are examples. Because a holder can crash or pause, each lock is in practice a lease, and safety needs fencing at the resource.
Extending a lease before it expires. Holders renew well before the deadline, often every third of the lease or more often, so that one or two failed renewals don't lose it.
A task scheduled to run automatically at set times, named after the Unix cron scheduler.
A Kubernetes API object in the coordination.k8s.io group that controllers renew to hold leadership; it is stored in etcd behind the API server.
The component that every part of Kubernetes talks to; it validates requests and stores cluster state in etcd.
The distributed file system of the Hadoop ecosystem. Its highly available NameNode setup uses ZooKeeper to elect the active NameNode.
A collection of articles by Amazon engineers on how AWS builds and operates distributed systems, covering timeouts, retries, leader election and more.
A bug where a program checks a condition and then acts on it, but the condition changes in between, for example a lease expiring during a pause after the check.
A researcher and author of Designing Data-Intensive Applications. His 2016 article on distributed locking criticised Redlock and popularised fencing tokens.
A counter on each ZooKeeper znode that increases whenever its children change; ZooKeeper uses it to number sequential znodes.
The number of rows an UPDATE or DELETE statement changed. Zero after a conditional update means the condition failed, for example because you were fenced off.
A lock used only to avoid duplicate work; an occasional second holder wastes resources but harms nothing. A single Redis node is enough.
A lock whose failure would corrupt data, double-charge or lose updates. It needs a consensus-backed lock service plus fencing at the resource.
Options of the Redis SET command: NX sets the key only if it doesn’t exist yet, and PX gives it an expiry in milliseconds. Together they acquire a simple lock with a timeout.
example: SET lock:report a7f NX PX 30000 takes the lock for 30 seconds if nobody holds it.

definition: An algorithm proposed by Redis’s creator for a lock across several independent Redis instances: acquire on a majority within the key’s time to live. Kleppmann argued it is unsafe for correctness because it has no fencing tokens and depends on timing.
The Italian programmer who created Redis, known online as antirez. He proposed Redlock and defended it against Kleppmann’s critique.
In Redlock, how long the client may treat the lock as held: the key’s time to live minus the time acquisition took, minus an allowance for clock drift.
A set of consumers sharing a Kafka topic, where each partition is read by exactly one member at a time. Ownership moves in a rebalance when members join or leave.
An etcd request of the form "if these comparisons hold, then do these operations, else those", executed atomically. It can check a lock key’s revision and write data in one step.
A payment processing company whose API supports idempotency keys on requests.
A Dutch payment processing company whose API supports idempotency keys.
Detecting and discarding repeated copies of the same message or request, usually by remembering ids already processed. Needed whenever delivery is at least once.
Only ever going up. A strictly increasing number never repeats or goes down, which is what a fencing token or a Raft term needs.
Getting several participants to all commit a transaction or all abort it. Unlike consensus, a single "no" vote must abort everything.

A variant of two-phase commit (Skeen, 1981) that adds a pre-commit phase so participants can finish without the coordinator. It is non-blocking only if the network has bounded delays and failure detection is perfect, so it is rarely used.
A database or service taking part in an atomic commit. It votes yes or no when asked to prepare, then applies the coordinator’s decision.
The first phase of two-phase commit. A participant that votes yes first writes the transaction’s changes and a prepare record durably and keeps its locks; it then can no longer abort on its own.
The moment a distributed transaction’s outcome becomes final: in two-phase commit, when the coordinator durably logs its COMMIT record.
The coordinator’s logged decision in two-phase commit. Once COMMIT is written the transaction must commit everywhere; ABORT, or no record at all, means it must abort.
A two-phase commit convention: if a restarted coordinator finds no decision record, it aborts, because no participant can have been told to commit. Only COMMIT records then need forcing to disk.
A transaction at a participant that has voted yes but not yet learned the decision. It must keep its locks and wait, which is the blocking problem.
A protocol in which one node’s failure can leave others stuck waiting indefinitely. Two-phase commit is blocking: in-doubt participants hold locks until the coordinator returns.

PostgreSQL’s support for being a two-phase commit participant: PREPARE TRANSACTION makes a transaction durable but undecided, and COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED finishes it. It is off by default (max_prepared_transactions = 0).
PostgreSQL’s maintenance process that reclaims space from old row versions. A forgotten prepared transaction stops it cleaning up.
The X/Open standard interface that lets a transaction manager run two-phase commit across databases and message queues from different vendors.
A write that must reach the disk (for example with fsync) before the protocol continues, so it survives a crash. They are a large part of two-phase commit’s cost.
A CockroachDB protocol that overlaps the two phases of its distributed commit, so a typical transaction commits after one round of consensus writes.
The three phases of three-phase commit: ask whether participants can commit, tell them to prepare to commit, then tell them to commit.
The procedure surviving participants run after a coordinator fails to agree the outcome among themselves, for example by asking a participant that already knows the decision.

A long-running business operation split into a sequence of local transactions, each committed straight away in its own service. If a step fails, earlier steps are undone with compensating transactions (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987).
example: Create order, reserve stock, charge card; if the charge fails, release the stock and cancel the order.

definition: A transaction inside a single database or service, with ordinary ACID guarantees. Sagas chain them together.
A new action that semantically undoes an earlier completed step, such as a refund for a charge. It must be idempotent and safe even if the original step never happened.
The go/no-go step of a saga: once it succeeds the saga must complete, and steps after it are only retried, never undone.
A saga step after the pivot that is retried until it succeeds rather than compensated, such as sending a confirmation email.
A saga step that can be undone by a compensating transaction, placed before the pivot.
Running a saga from a central orchestrator, a durable state machine that tells each service what to do and handles failures. The whole flow is visible in one place.
Running a saga with no central controller: each service reacts to events from others and publishes its own. Simple for short flows, hard to follow for long ones.
Amazon’s managed workflow service that runs durable state machines, often used to orchestrate sagas.
A workflow and process-automation platform that runs BPMN process models, used to orchestrate long-running business processes.
Running workflow code so that its progress is saved at each step and it resumes where it left off after a crash, even days later. Temporal is an example.
Software that runs multi-step processes, tracking each one’s state, timers and retries durably.
An anomaly where two concurrent read-modify-write cycles both start from the same value, so one overwrites the other’s change.
Reading data another transaction has written but not finally committed, which may later be undone.
An application-level flag, such as a PENDING status, marking a record as part of an unfinished saga so other operations treat it carefully.
A pattern for updating a database and publishing an event atomically: write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, and let a separate relay publish it afterwards.
Reading a database’s change log (such as its write-ahead log) and turning each change into an event for other systems.
A delivery guarantee in which every message arrives, possibly more than once. Consumers must deduplicate.
A guarantee that each message is processed once and only once. Networks can’t provide it directly; systems approximate it with at-least-once delivery plus deduplication.
The risk when a service writes to two systems (such as its database and a message broker) separately: a crash between them leaves them inconsistent.
A temporary failure, such as a timeout or a brief overload, that is likely to succeed if retried. A declined card is a business failure, not a transient one.
Replication in which several nodes accept writes for the same data and exchange them with each other, so concurrent conflicting writes must be merged.
An app design that works fully without a network connection, storing changes locally and syncing them later, so its local copy is a replica that must merge.
One version vector dominates another if it is greater than or equal in every entry. The dominated version is out of date and can be discarded.
example: {A:2, B:3} dominates {A:2, B:1}.

definition: A CRDT whose replicas exchange their whole state and combine it with a merge that is commutative, associative and idempotent, so states can be delivered in any order, any number of times.
A CRDT whose replicas broadcast operations rather than state. Concurrent operations must commute, and delivery usually has to be exactly once and in causal order.
A state-based CRDT that ships only the recently changed part of its state, merged with the same join, saving bandwidth.
An operation is associative when grouping doesn’t change the result: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
The guarantee CRDTs give: any two replicas that have received the same set of updates are in the same state, with no conflict resolution needed.
A set with a partial order in which any two elements have a least upper bound (their join): the smallest element at or above both. A state-based CRDT’s merge computes this join.
example: With "take the larger number", the join of 3 and 5 is 5.

definition: An update that only moves a CRDT’s state upwards in its order, so merging the new state with the old gives the new state. Deleting is not inflationary, which is why removes become tombstones.
A CRDT counter in which each replica increments only its own entry in a vector; the value is the sum of the entries and merge takes the element-wise maximum.
example: [A:3, B:2, C:0] has value 5.

definition: A CRDT counter that supports decrements by keeping two G-Counters, P for increments and N for decrements; its value is sum(P) − sum(N).
example: P totalling 8 and N totalling 3 give a value of 5.

definition: A counter whose available quantity is divided between replicas in advance, so each can decrement its own share without coordinating and the total can never go below zero.
example: 60 units of stock to the EU replica and 40 to the US replica.

definition: Combining two vectors by taking the larger value in each position separately.
example: The element-wise maximum of [4, 1, 0] and [2, 3, 0] is [4, 3, 0].

definition: A CRDT set that only supports adding; merge is set union.
A CRDT set made of an add-set and a remove-set (tombstones); an element is present if added and not removed. Once removed it can never be added again.
The rule that when an add and a remove of the same element happen concurrently, the element stays in the set. OR-Sets behave this way.
Combining two sets into one containing every element of either. It is commutative, associative and idempotent, so it is a valid CRDT merge.
CRDT registers holding one value. An LWW-Register keeps the write with the highest (timestamp, replica id); an MV-Register keeps all concurrent values for the reader to resolve.
A CRDT for ordered lists such as text, used for collaborative editing. RGA and Logoot are early designs; Yjs and Automerge are widely used libraries.
An open-source CRDT library for building collaborative editors and apps in JavaScript.
An open-source CRDT library for local-first apps that stores documents as JSON-like data and merges concurrent edits.
The active-active geo-replication in Redis Enterprise, where a database replicated across regions is called a conflict-free replicated database (CRDB) and its counters and sets are CRDTs.
An "observed-remove set without tombstones" used in Riak. It tracks causality with version vectors so removed elements can be forgotten instead of kept as tombstones.

A way of spreading information in which each node periodically picks a random peer and exchanges state, so news spreads like an infection, reaching all N nodes in about log N rounds with constant load per node.
example: With one exchange per second, a change reaches about 1,000 nodes in roughly 17 seconds.

definition: In gossip, how many peers each node contacts per round.
Gossip styles: in push, informed nodes send news to random peers; in pull, nodes ask random peers for news; push-pull does both, finishing the last stragglers much faster.
A compact summary, such as version numbers or hashes, that two nodes exchange first so they send each other only the entries that differ.
A measure of how spread out values are: the average squared distance from the mean.
The square root of the variance, in the same units as the data; a measure of typical spread around the mean.
The time between one event and the next, such as between consecutive heartbeats.
The probability that a random value is further out than some threshold, such as a heartbeat arriving more than t seconds late.

The output of a phi accrual detector: minus the base-10 logarithm of the modelled chance that a healthy node would be this quiet. Phi 1 means a 10% chance, 3 means 0.1%; Cassandra convicts a node at phi_convict_threshold, 8 by default.
A toolkit for building concurrent and distributed applications on the JVM; its cluster module uses a phi accrual failure detector.

A scalable membership and failure-detection protocol (Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002): each node pings a random peer each period, asks others to probe it indirectly if there is no reply, and spreads suspicions and updates by piggybacking them on its messages.
SWIM’s indirect probe: node A asks other members to ping B for it when B didn’t answer A’s own ping.
An intermediate state in SWIM in which an unresponsive member is suspected but not yet declared dead, giving it time to refute the suspicion.
A counter a SWIM member increases to refute a suspicion about itself; a message with a higher incarnation number overrides older suspicions.
Attaching extra information, such as membership updates, to messages that are being sent anyway, so it spreads with no separate traffic.
HashiCorp’s Go library implementing SWIM-based membership and failure detection, used in Consul, Nomad and Serf.
A software company that makes infrastructure tools including Terraform, Consul, Nomad and Vault.
HashiCorp’s scheduler for running containers and other workloads across a cluster.
HashiCorp’s tool for cluster membership, failure detection and event broadcast, built on memberlist.
HashiCorp’s extensions to SWIM that reduce false positives caused by slow or overloaded members, for example by having a node that suspects its own slowness wait longer.
